title: Beshalach: Joseph's bones (Exodus 13:19)
hookLine: while others gather silver, Moses carries Joseph's bones, keeping an old promise
last: THE LONG WAY CAN BE KINDER.

lines: MOVING DAY, A HUNDRED YEARS ON.
cards: Picture moving day after a hundred years in the same house. Everyone grabs what matters: the good dishes, the jewelry, the papers.
And one person is up in the attic, looking for something nobody else remembers: a promise made long before any of them were born.
The Israelites are leaving Egypt in a hurry, and the Torah stops, mid-march, for one short verse about what Moses chose to pack.

teach.b: "And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him." That's the verse. To hear why it matters, go back to the end of Genesis.
Joseph, dying in Egypt, made his brothers swear: when God remembers you and brings you out, carry my bones up with you. Generations passed. Slavery came.
Most people must have forgotten. Moses didn't. The Talmud sets a scene around the verse.
On the night of leaving, the Israelites were busy with the silver and gold the Egyptians had given them; the Torah does say they asked for jewels of silver and gold, and received them.
But Moses, the Talmud says, was busy with Joseph's bones, and it quotes a line from Proverbs about him: the wise in heart takes on commandments. Everyone else carried treasure. He carried a promise.

The rabbis tell more: Joseph's coffin had been sunk in the Nile, and an old woman named Serach, Joseph's niece, remembered where. That part is midrash, a story the tradition tells, not the plain text.
The plain text finishes the arc much later.

teach.h: SILVER FOR THEM, BONES FOR MOSES.
teach.b: In the book of Joshua, Joseph's bones are buried at Shechem, in the land.
A promise made by brothers, kept by a descendant of one of them, finished by a generation not yet born.
And the Hebrew word for bone, etzem, also means essence, the self. Moses carried Joseph's very self out of Egypt.

how: Jewish tradition treats keeping one's word as weighty, and promises to the dying especially so; Moses carrying Joseph's bones is often taught as the model of a promise kept across generations.

o: they went out: the Hebrew name for the Exodus
the march: a word for a people on the move
when he let go: the opening words of the portion

games.q: who carried what — tap the pairs.

s: Joseph asked to be carried out of Egypt when he died
at the end of Genesis he made his brothers swear to carry his bones up.
the story of Serach finding the coffin is in the plain text of Exodus
it's midrash, a story the tradition tells, found in the Talmud.
Joseph's bones were buried in the land, at Shechem
the book of Joshua finishes the arc, generations later.

games.q: the night of leaving Egypt. everyone is packing silver and gold. you're Moses. what does the Talmud say you're busy with?
games.why: the bones of Joseph. the Talmud applies to him a line from Proverbs: the wise in heart takes on commandments.

practice: Let one old promise come up, even a small one: a call you meant to make, a recipe you meant to learn, the town your grandfather came from. Don't judge how long it has waited; Joseph's waited a long time too.
Just hold it, and ask what one step would carry it a little further.

wordCard.voice: Beshalach. When he let go. Our portion, where Moses leaves Egypt carrying Joseph's bones, an old promise kept.

orig.note: Hebrew: bones. the singular, etzem, also means essence, the self.

carryVoice: Your line: carry the bones. Some promises take generations to keep. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.
